bridge: Builds on C06 process identity, L02 shell concepts and S06 permissions. Windows observation is optional if unavailable; the synthetic event exercise is platform-independent.
teaching:
Read the synthetic example before thinking about system logs. $events names a variable; @(...) makes an array. [pscustomobject]@{...} creates one object with named properties. The pipe | sends those objects to the next command. Where-Object keeps objects matching a condition; -eq means equal. Select-Object chooses the properties to display. Nothing in this fixture reads or changes your computer’s logs.

PowerShell processes objects through pipelines rather than only lines of text. Select properties and filter on their types. A displayed table can omit fields or truncate values, so preserve structured output when it matters to evidence.

Windows events have providers, event IDs, timestamps and fields whose meaning depends on source/configuration. An ID without provider/context is not a complete analytic definition. Process identity, integrity and privileges also influence which actions are possible. Inspect only your own lab activity and avoid exporting personal event data into shared notes.

Start with a synthetic object so the query is reproducible on paper as well as in PowerShell. Learn the distinction between filtering before collection, filtering objects and formatting output. Formatting is a final presentation step, not a replacement for retaining the underlying structured evidence.

PowerShell normally passes structured objects between cmdlets, so sort and filter properties before formatting for display. Use full names such as Get-ChildItem and Get-Process in saved scripts; an alias familiar from another shell may have different parameters or may not exist on another platform. Inspect $PSVersionTable to record your engine version. Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 can differ in module support. Keep the beginner exercise read-only and avoid elevated shells or downloaded bootstrap scripts. Registry views and on-disk hive files are related but are not interchangeable copies of every live registry entry.
example:
# PowerShell synthetic objects; no system logs read
$events = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=1;User='A';Result='Fail'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=2;User='A';Result='OK'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=3;User='B';Result='Fail'}
)
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Select-Object Id,User
# Expected records: 1/A and3/B
explanation: The query filters the Result property, then projects Id and User. It does not search a rendered text table for a substring. On a non-Windows machine without PowerShell, manually apply the same predicates and label the runtime check unperformed.
exercise: Run or hand-trace the supplied objects. Filter failed events for user A only, then count failures by user. Record input records and expected output separately from any optional host observations.
solution:
The A-only failure is Id 1. Add these lines after the supplied $events array if PowerShell is available; otherwise trace the same conditions on paper.

```powershell
$events | Where-Object { $_.Result -eq 'Fail' -and $_.User -eq 'A' } | Select-Object Id,User
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Group-Object User | Select-Object Name,Count
```

Inside the braces, $_ means the current object and -and requires both conditions. Group-Object collects matching User values; the groups are A with Count 1 and B with Count 1. These are synthetic counts, not findings about an actual endpoint.
challenge: Explain what additional metadata a real event record needs for an investigation: provider/source, time/offset, host, collection provenance and field schema. Give one reason a missing event might not prove the activity never occurred.
challenge_solution: Logging can be disabled, filtered, rotated or uncollected. Event meaning requires source/schema and time context. A sound answer distinguishes missing visibility from evidence of absence.
